Quantitative Microbiome Profiling: Absolute Abundances from a Measured Load

Source: R/qmp.r
qmp.Rd

Turn relative abundances into estimates of absolute abundance, using each sample's measured total microbial load (flow cytometry cell counts, total 16S qPCR, a spike-in, DNA yield, ...).

Usage

qmp_scale(counts, load, data = NULL, margin = 1L, cpus = n_cpus())

qmp_rarefy(counts, load, data = NULL, margin = 1L, seed = 0L, cpus = n_cpus())

Arguments

counts

A count table (samples \(\times\) features); see Input Types. qmp_rarefy() needs whole numbers (integer counts).

load

The total microbial load of each sample, in any absolute unit (cells per gram, 16S copies per µl, ...): finite and greater than 0. A numeric vector with one value per sample, matched to the samples by name when both are named, else in the samples' order. Or, when data is given, the name of one of its columns (or a vector with one value per row of data).

data

Optional sample metadata: a data frame with one row per sample, holding load as a column. Rows are matched to the samples in counts by row name, and rows for other samples are ignored; without row names, they must be in the same order as the samples. Default: NULL.

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

seed

An integer seed for the random rarefaction. The same seed gives the same result, for any cpus. Default: 0.

Value

A table of absolute abundances (doubles), in the form of counts, as normalize() returns it: the same orientation and dimnames, a base matrix for a base matrix, the same Matrix class (dgCMatrix, dgTMatrix, dgeMatrix) or a slam simple_triplet_matrix for those, with zeros not stored; and a phyloseq, rbiom, or SummarizedExperiment object gives its count matrix. Each sample's values sum to its load.

qmp_rarefy()'s result also has attributes sampling_depth (each sample's \(s_i\)) and target (its \(t_i\), the number of reads it was rarefied to), named by sample. They are attached to every class, sparse ones too, but subsetting or converting a Matrix or slam object drops them, so read them first.

Details

  • qmp_scale(): "relative abundance \(\times\) load" (Jian et al. 2020; most qPCR and spike-in studies). Each sample's counts are divided by its total and multiplied by its load: $$q_{ij} = x_{ij} / n_i \times L_i$$

  • qmp_rarefy(): quantitative microbiome profiling as published by Vandeputte et al. (2017). Each sample is first rarefied to the same sampling depth relative to its load (reads per cell), so that every sample has the same detection limit in absolute units, then scaled to its load. The steps follow the authors' script, QMP.R:

    1. Each sample's sampling depth is \(s_i = n_i / L_i\), its total number of reads over its load.

    2. \(s_{min} = \min_i s_i\).

    3. Sample \(i\) is rarefied, without replacement, to \(t_i = \lfloor s_{min} L_i \rfloor\) reads (so \(t_i \le n_i\); the sample with the smallest \(s_i\) keeps all its reads).

    4. The rarefied counts \(r_{ij}\) are scaled to the load: \(q_{ij} = r_{ij} / t_i \times L_i\).

Before and after

  • Neither method makes the data less noisy. The error of the load measurement carries straight into every taxon (Vandeputte et al. 2017; Props et al. 2017): measure load in replicate.

  • 16S copy-number correction (dividing each taxon's counts by its 16S gene copy number) is a separate, earlier step in Vandeputte's pipeline, and isn't part of either function. Do it with sweep() (see the examples). The authors' script then rounds the corrected table up with ceiling(); qmp_rarefy() requires whole numbers instead, so call qmp_rarefy(ceiling(x), load) to do as the script does.

  • Spike-ins: the load is usually spike_added * total_reads / spike_reads. Drop the spike-in feature from counts before calling qmp_*().

  • The results are absolute abundances, not compositions. Don't follow them with a centred log ratio (norm = 'clr'), which removes the load again. Bray-Curtis on QMP data is the usual next step: bray() or beta_div() with norm = 'none'.

Differences from QMP.R

qmp_rarefy() follows rarefy_even_sampling_depth() in the authors' QMP.R (BSD-3, © 2017 Raes Lab), except:

  • It doesn't apply ceiling() to counts; non-integer counts are an error.

  • Targets \(s_{min} L_i\) are floored (as the script's call to phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth() does), but a value within \(10^{-9}\) (relative) of a whole number counts as that number, so that floating-point rounding never costs a read; the sample with the smallest sampling depth keeps all its reads.

  • A sample whose target is 0 reads (a load so small that \(s_{min} L_i < 1\)) is an error, naming it, where the script returns NaNs. So is an empty sample.

  • Rarefaction uses ecodive's own rarefy() code and seed, so the random draws differ from the script's (rngseed = 711), while the sampling depths, targets, and totals are the same.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

References

Vandeputte, D., Kathagen, G., D'hoe, K., et al. (2017). Quantitative microbiome profiling links gut community variation to microbial load. Nature, 551, 507–511. doi:10.1038/nature24460

Jian, C., Luukkonen, P., Yki-Järvinen, H., Salonen, A., & Korpela, K. (2020). Quantitative PCR provides a simple and accessible method for quantitative microbiota profiling. PLoS ONE, 15, e0227285. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0227285

Props, R., Kerckhof, F.-M., Rubbens, P., et al. (2017). Absolute quantification of microbial taxon abundances. The ISME Journal, 11, 584–587. doi:10.1038/ismej.2016.117

See also

normalize(), rarefy(), and the compositional methods, which recover only ratios when no load was measured: alr(), log_ratio(), rho_p(), replace_zeros().

Examples

    # Cell counts per gram for each sample of ex_counts.
    load <- c(Saliva = 2.0e10, Gums = 4.1e10, Nose = 1.0e10, Stool = 3.2e10)

    # Relative abundance x load
    q <- qmp_scale(ex_counts, load)
    q[1:3, 1:3]
#>        Streptococcus Bacteroides Corynebacterium
#> Saliva    9391304348   115942029               0
#> Gums     36696388262   185101580               0
#> Nose       217606330    19782394      4925816024
    all.equal(rowSums(q), load)
#> [1] TRUE

    # Vandeputte et al.'s QMP: rarefy to an even sampling depth first
    q <- qmp_rarefy(ex_counts, load)
    q[1:3, 1:3]
#>        Streptococcus Bacteroides Corynebacterium
#> Saliva    9391304348   115942029               0
#> Gums     36766619519   173974540               0
#> Nose       232558140           0      4941860465
    attr(q, 'sampling_depth')[1:3]  # reads per cell
#>       Saliva         Gums         Nose 
#> 1.725000e-08 2.160976e-08 1.011000e-07 
    attr(q, 'target')[1:3]          # reads kept
#> Saliva   Gums   Nose 
#>    345    707    172 

    # The load as a column of sample metadata
    meta <- data.frame(cells = load, row.names = names(load))
    q <- qmp_scale(ex_counts, 'cells', data = meta)

    # 16S copy-number correction comes first, as in the authors' script
    copies <- seq(1, 4, length.out = ncol(ex_counts))  # per taxon
    x <- sweep(ex_counts, 2, copies, '/')
    q <- qmp_rarefy(ceiling(x), load)

    # Usually followed by Bray-Curtis distances
    dm <- bray(qmp_rarefy(ex_counts, load))
